claim: Case fatality rates in severe falciparum malaria depend on the pattern and degree of vital organ dysfunction.
source: Case fatality rates in severe falciparum malaria depend on the pattern and degree of vital organ dysfunction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Recent large-scale case-control analyses of pooled severe malaria data reported that glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDd) was protective against cerebral malaria.
source: Recent large-scale case-control analyses of pooled severe malaria data reported that glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDd) was protective against cerebral malaria but increased the risk of severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This references findings from prior studies (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2014; Clarke et al., 2017) that are being re-analyzed in this manuscript.

claim: Recent large-scale case-control analyses of pooled severe malaria data reported that G6PDd increased the risk of severe malarial anaemia.
source: Recent large-scale case-control analyses of pooled severe malaria data reported that glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDd) was protective against cerebral malaria but increased the risk of severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This references findings from prior studies that are being re-analyzed.

claim: A novel formulation of the balancing selection hypothesis was proposed whereby the selective advantage is driven by the competing risks of death from cerebral malaria and death from severe malarial anaemia.
source: A novel formulation of the balancing selection hypothesis was proposed as an explanation for these findings, whereby the selective advantage is driven by the competing risks of death from cerebral malaria and death from severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This references a hypothesis proposed in Clarke et al. (2017).

claim: The claims about G6PDd being protective against cerebral malaria are subject to collider bias.
source: We re-analysed these claims using causal diagrams and showed that they are subject to collider bias.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current manuscript, supported by simulation analysis and causal diagrams presented in the results.

claim: Collider bias is sufficient to explain all of the observed association between G6PDd and cerebral malaria.
source: A simulation based sensitivity analysis, varying the strength of the known effect of G6PDd on anaemia, showed that this bias is sufficient to explain all of the observed association.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Severe falciparum malaria is defined by one or more criteria indicating vital organ dysfunction in the presence of microscopy confirmed asexual blood stages of Plasmodium falciparum in the peripheral blood film.
source: Severe falciparum malaria is defined by one or more criteria indicating vital organ dysfunction in the presence of microscopy confirmed asexual blood stages of Plasmodium falciparum in the peripheral blood film (WHO, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: Multiple vital organ dysfunction is associated with increased mortality in severe malaria.
source: Multiple vital organ dysfunction is associated with increased mortality (WHO, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO documentation.

claim: Common major clinical manifestations of severe malaria include coma, acidosis, renal failure and anaemia.
source: Common major clinical manifestations of severe malaria include coma, acidosis, renal failure and anaemia.
evidence: This is stated as established medical knowledge.

claim: Anaemia is an inevitable consequence of symptomatic malaria.
source: Of these manifestations, anaemia is an inevitable consequence of symptomatic malaria (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Anaemia in individuals at risk of Plasmodium falciparum infection can be the consequence of red cell genetic polymorphisms such as G6PDd or haemoglobinopathies.
source: However, anaemia in individuals at risk of Plasmodium falciparum infection can also be the consequence of red cell genetic polymorphisms frequent in the populations at risk, such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDd) or haemoglobinopathies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about genetic factors affecting anaemia.

claim: There is considerable interest in understanding the mechanisms conferring protective effects against severe falciparum malaria of genetic polymorphisms common in malaria endemic areas.
source: There is considerable interest in understanding the mechanisms conferring protective effects against severe falciparum malaria of the genetic polymorphisms which are common in malaria endemic areas (Weatherall, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: For sickle cell trait, several different protective mechanisms have been proposed including reduced parasite erythrocyte invasion, enhanced parasitised red cell phagocytosis and a reduced propensity of infected red cells to sequester in the microvasculature.
source: For some, such as the sickle cell trait, several different mechanisms have been proposed. These include reduced parasite erythrocyte invasion, enhanced parasitised red cell phagocytosis and a reduced propensity of infected red cells to sequester in the microvasculature (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2014; Band et al., 2015; Cholera et al., 2008; Williams, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mechanism underlying protection from severe falciparum malaria is less clear for G6PDd.
source: The mechanism underlying protection from severe falciparum malaria is less clear for others such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PDd).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: G6PDd is an X-linked genetic polymorphism that results in the most common human enzymopathy.
source: This X-linked genetic polymorphism results in the most common human enzymopathy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about G6PDd.

claim: Nearly 200 different genetic variants of G6PD have been reported.
source: Nearly 200 different genetic variants have been reported (Howes et al., 2012; Luzzatto and Arese, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The mechanism whereby G6PD deficiency protects against malaria is still debated.
source: The mechanism whereby G6PD deficiency protects against malaria, and the natural selection forces which have resulted in the different genotypes are still debated.
evidence: This is stated as an ongoing debate in the field.

claim: The natural selection forces which have resulted in the different G6PD genotypes are still debated.
source: The mechanism whereby G6PD deficiency protects against malaria, and the natural selection forces which have resulted in the different genotypes are still debated.
evidence: This is stated as an ongoing debate in the field.

claim: Prospective observational hospital or clinic based patient studies have provided the major component of the evidence base for G6PD and malaria.
source: Prospective observational hospital or clinic based patient studies have provided the major component of the evidence base.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the existing evidence base.

claim: Estimating causal effects from observational studies in severe malaria patients is difficult due to both confounding and selection bias.
source: Estimating causal effects from observational studies in severe malaria patients is difficult due to both confounding and selection bias.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological challenge in the field.

claim: The work focuses on collider bias introduced by inappropriate data filtering.
source: This work focuses on collider bias introduced by inappropriate data filtering (Snoep et al., 2014; Pearce and Richiardi, 2014).
evidence: This is the stated focus of the manuscript, with citations to relevant methodological literature.

claim: Previous studies suggested that G6PDd both increases the risk of severe malarial anaemia (SMA) and decreases the risk of cerebral malaria (CM).
source: It has been suggested that G6PDd both increases the risk of severe malarial anaemia (SMA) and decreases the risk of cerebral malaria (CM) (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2014; Clarke et al., 2017).
evidence: This references findings from prior studies.

claim: The conclusions about G6PDd effects were based on a pooled analysis of observational data from over 11,000 patients with severe malaria studied in Africa and Asia, and relevant population controls.
source: These conclusions were based on a pooled analysis of observational data from over 11,000 patients with severe malaria studied in Africa and Asia, and relevant population controls.
evidence: This describes the data source for the prior studies being re-analyzed.

claim: Based on genetic association studies, a new formulation of the balancing-selection hypothesis was proposed in which G6PD polymorphisms are maintained in human populations by an evolutionary trade-off between different adverse outcomes of P. falciparum infection.
source: Based on these genetic association studies, a new formulation of the balancing-selection hypothesis was proposed in which G6PD polymorphisms are maintained in human populations, at least in part, by an evolutionary trade-off between different adverse outcomes of P. falciparum infection (Clarke et al., 2017).
evidence: This references a hypothesis from Clarke et al. (2017).

claim: Collider bias probably explains the negative association between G6PDd and CM.
source: Collider bias probably explains this negative association between G6PDd and CM, suggesting that causal interpretations of this association and the novel formulation of balancing selection in G6PDd are invalid.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by the simulation analysis.

claim: Causal interpretations of the association between G6PDd and CM and the novel formulation of balancing selection in G6PDd are invalid.
source: Collider bias probably explains this negative association between G6PDd and CM, suggesting that causal interpretations of this association and the novel formulation of balancing selection in G6PDd are invalid.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: Two published analyses of pooled data from observational studies of patients with severe falciparum malaria used severe malarial anaemia (SMA) and cerebral malaria (CM) as the main endpoints.
source: Two published analyses of pooled data from observational studies of patients with severe falciparum malaria used severe malarial anaemia (SMA) and cerebral malaria (CM) as the main endpoints (outcomes) of interest (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2014; Clarke et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodology of the prior studies.

claim: Both published analyses defined cases of CM as the presence of coma but without concomitant SMA.
source: Both these published analyses defined cases of CM as the presence of coma but without concomitant SMA, and cases of SMA as patients with severe anaemia but who were conscious.
evidence: This describes the case definitions used in the prior studies.

claim: Both published analyses defined cases of SMA as patients with severe anaemia but who were conscious.
source: Both these published analyses defined cases of CM as the presence of coma but without concomitant SMA, and cases of SMA as patients with severe anaemia but who were conscious.
evidence: This describes the case definitions used in the prior studies.

claim: The case definitions excluded patients who had both SMA and CM.
source: Therefore, these case definitions excluded patients who had both SMA and CM.
evidence: This is an inference from the case definitions described.

claim: All other presentations of severe malaria were excluded (pulmonary oedema, shock, etc.).
source: All other presentations of severe malaria were also excluded (pulmonary oedema, shock, etc.).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria of the prior studies.

claim: Population controls were recruited at each site to match the ethnic composition of cases.
source: Population controls were recruited at each site to match the ethnic composition of cases, and in some instances cord blood samples were used as controls.
evidence: This describes the control selection in the prior studies.

claim: In some instances cord blood samples were used as controls.
source: Population controls were recruited at each site to match the ethnic composition of cases, and in some instances cord blood samples were used as controls.
evidence: This describes the control selection in the prior studies.

claim: The consequence of these case definitions is to create an artificial dependency between SMA and CM: if a patient has SMA then they cannot have CM.
source: The consequence of these case definitions is to create an artificial dependency between SMA and CM: if a patient has SMA then they cannot have CM.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the case definitions.

claim: G6PDd is known to influence haemoglobin concentrations directly by causing haemolysis of older erythrocytes in acute malaria.
source: G6PDd is known to influence haemoglobin concentrations directly by causing haemolysis of older erythrocytes in acute malaria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about G6PDd.

claim: It is to be expected that SMA is positively correlated with G6PDd, thus creating a negative correlation between CM and G6PDd.
source: Therefore it is to be expected that SMA is positively correlated with G6PDd, thus creating a negative correlation between CM and G6PDd.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the known effect of G6PDd on anaemia and the case definitions.

claim: The mean G6PDd score was 13.5% in controls, 13% in cerebral malaria cases and 16.9% in severe malarial anaemia cases.
source: Indeed, when all the G6PDd mutations were mapped onto the WHO severity classification score (Yoshida et al., 1971), it was observed that "The mean G6PDd score was 13.5% in controls, 13% in cerebral malaria cases and 16.9% in severe malarial anaemia cases [..]." (page 8, Clarke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is data from Clarke et al. (2017).

claim: After exclusion of the G6PD c.202C > T mutation, the pattern of G6PDd scores remained consistent (6, 5.6, and 7.1%, respectively for controls, CM cases, and SMA cases).
source: This pattern remained consistent (6, 5.6, and 7.1%, respectively) after exclusion of the G6PD c.202C > T mutation (one of the 'A-' mutations and the most prevalent in the pooled data).
evidence: This is data from Clarke et al. (2017).

claim: By excluding patients with both SMA and CM (approximately 12% of those with either SMA or CM in the pooled data), the number of G6PDd patients in the CM category is artificially reduced.
source: By excluding patients with both SMA and CM (approximately 12% of those with either SMA or CM in the pooled data), the number of G6PDd patients in the CM category is artificially reduced and we would expect there to be fewer G6PDd patients than in the control group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the case definitions and the known effect of G6PDd on SMA.

claim: We would expect there to be fewer G6PDd patients in the CM category than in the control group due to the exclusion of patients with both SMA and CM.
source: By excluding patients with both SMA and CM (approximately 12% of those with either SMA or CM in the pooled data), the number of G6PDd patients in the CM category is artificially reduced and we would expect there to be fewer G6PDd patients than in the control group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the case definitions and collider bias.

claim: Figure 1 proposes a simple causal diagram which posits plausible inter-dependencies limited to the variables of interest.
source: Figure 1 proposes a simple causal diagram which posits plausible inter-dependencies limited to the variables of interest.
evidence: This refers to the causal diagram presented in Figure 1.

claim: A simple simulation study based on the assumptions shown in Figure 1 can be used to estimate the relationship between G6PDd and SMA which would result in the observed odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls.
source: A simple simulation study based on the assumptions shown in Figure 1 can be used to estimate the relationship between G6PDd and SMA which would result in the observed odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls reported in Clarke et al. (2017).
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology used in the manuscript.

claim: The null model assessed assumes there is no direct causal link between G6PDd and CM in severe falciparum malaria.
source: We assessed the null model in which there is no direct causal link between G6PDd and CM in severe falciparum malaria (i.e. no arrow from G6PD deficiency to CM).
evidence: This describes the null hypothesis tested in the simulation.

claim: The simulation assumes there is no direct link between SMA and CM.
source: We also assume that there is no direct link between SMA and CM.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the simulation model.

claim: The model was calibrated with the marginal probabilities of SMA and CM reported in Clarke et al. (2017).
source: We calibrated the model with the marginal probabilities of SMA and CM reported in Clarke et al. (2017) and only varied the odds ratio of G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls from 1 (assuming no effect of G6PDd on SMA) to 2 (twice as likely to be G6PDd in the SMA cases than in the controls).
evidence: This describes the calibration of the simulation model.

claim: The analysis was restricted to males to avoid assumptions concerning gene dose effects.
source: For simplicity (avoiding assumptions concerning gene dose effects) we restricted the analysis to males and only compare the simulation results with the reported associations in males.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the analysis.

claim: If the odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls is strictly greater than 1, the estimated odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls is biased.
source: Figure 2 shows that if the odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls is strictly greater than 1, the estimated odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls is biased (the thick red line is below the true simulated value of 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The magnitude of the bias in the estimated odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls increases monotonically as the odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls increases.
source: The magnitude of this bias increases monotonically as the odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls increases.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: There is no bias in the estimated odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls.
source: As can be seen from the causal diagram in Figure 1, there is no bias in the estimated odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls (in Figure 2 the thick blue line approximates the identity line).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: For any value of the odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls taken inside the reported 95% confidence interval [1.2–1.8] from Clarke et al. (2017), the simulation will result in a biased odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls inside the interval [0.69–0.98].
source: This simple simulation model, restricted to males, shows that for any value of the odds ratio for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls taken inside the reported 95% confidence interval (CI) [1.2–1.8] from Clarke et al. (2017), will result in a biased odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls inside the interval [0.69–0.98], the reported 95% CI for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls (Clarke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: Using the reported point estimate of 1.48 for the odds ratio of G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls (restricted to males), the simulation model estimates that the observed (biased) odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls is 0.87.
source: Moreover, if we use their reported point estimate of 1.48, restricted to males, for the odds ratio of G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls, the simulation model estimates that the observed (biased) odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls is 0.87, qualitatively very close to their estimate of 0.82.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: The simulated odds ratio of 0.87 is qualitatively very close to the Clarke et al. estimate of 0.82.
source: Moreover, if we use their reported point estimate of 1.48, restricted to males, for the odds ratio of G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls, the simulation model estimates that the observed (biased) odds ratio for G6PDd in CM cases versus controls is 0.87, qualitatively very close to their estimate of 0.82.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and prior study findings.

claim: The effect of G6PDd on severe anaemia in homozygous G6PDd girls and hemizygous G6PDd boys reported in Uyoga et al. (2015) was an odds ratio of 1.71 (95% CI: 1.34–2.18) for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls.
source: We note that the effect of G6PDd on severe anaemia in homozygous G6PDd girls and hemizygous G6PDd boys reported in Uyoga et al. (2015), an odds ratio of 1.71 (95% CI: 1.34–2.18) for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls, is also consistent with these results.
evidence: This cites data from Uyoga et al. (2015).

claim: The effect of G6PDd on severe anaemia reported in Uyoga et al. (2015) is consistent with the simulation results.
source: We note that the effect of G6PDd on severe anaemia in homozygous G6PDd girls and hemizygous G6PDd boys reported in Uyoga et al. (2015), an odds ratio of 1.71 (95% CI: 1.34–2.18) for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls, is also consistent with these results.
evidence: This is an inference comparing external data to the simulation results.

claim: The re-analysis of recent reports that G6PDd reduced the risk of CM directly suggests that the observations could have resulted entirely from collider bias.
source: This re-analysis of recent reports that G6PDd reduced the risk of CM directly (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2014; Clarke et al., 2017) suggests that the observations could have resulted entirely from collider bias.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: The findings highlight the difficulty of inferring causal relationships between baseline patient covariates and covariates which define inclusion criteria.
source: This highlights the difficulty of inferring causal relationships between baseline patient covariates (in this case G6PDd) and covariates which define inclusion criteria.
evidence: This is a general methodological conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The necessary causal odds ratios for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls which would give rise to the biased observed association between G6PD status and CM fit with the recent estimate of 1.71 in homozygous girls and hemizygous boys.
source: The necessary causal odds ratios for G6PDd in SMA cases versus controls which would give rise to the biased observed association between G6PD status and CM fit with the recent estimate of 1.71 in homozygous girls and hemizygous boys (Uyoga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing simulation results with external data.

claim: The observations reported could have arisen purely as a result of the implicit collider bias induced by the selection of patients by the severe malaria criteria.
source: This is not to say that the risk of CM is unaffected by G6PDd, but that the observations reported could have arisen purely as a result of the implicit collider bias induced by the selection of patients by the severe malaria criteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: All prospective observational severe malaria studies suffer from two major issues: case definitions are subjective and change over time, and mortality is strongly dependent on the case definition.
source: All prospective observational severe malaria studies suffer from two major issues. First, case definitions are subjective and change over time (even though standard guidelines exist, see WHO (2015)) and mortality is strongly dependent on the case definition.
evidence: This is stated as a general limitation of observational severe malaria studies.

claim: Enrolment into severe malaria studies can only be done at the hospital or clinic level and neither duration of illness nor treatment seeking behaviour can be accounted for adequately.
source: Second, enrolment into studies can only be done at the hospital or clinic level and neither duration of illness nor treatment seeking behaviour can be accounted for adequately.
evidence: This is stated as a general limitation of observational severe malaria studies.

claim: The notion and definition of 'severe malaria' has two operational purposes: it is a clinical tool for appropriate triage of malaria patients at high risk of death, and it is a research tool for the evaluation of novel interventions seeking to reduce mortality.
source: The notion and definition of 'severe malaria' has two operational purposes. First it is a clinical tool for appropriate triage of malaria patients at high risk of death. Second it is a research tool for the evaluation of novel interventions seeking to reduce mortality.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the purposes of the severe malaria definition.

claim: Interventions aimed at reducing mortality need to be trialled in the most severely ill patients in order to demonstrate intervention efficacy in this important subgroup.
source: Interventions aimed at reducing mortality need to be trialled in the most severely ill patients in order to demonstrate intervention efficacy in this important subgroup.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for studying severe malaria patients.

claim: Pooled analyses of severe malaria studies need to take into account the variability of study inclusion and exclusion criteria.
source: Pooled analyses of severe malaria studies need to take into account the variability of study inclusion and exclusion criteria.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: Researchers must appreciate that severe malaria is not an objective category but a subjective case definition subset from a spectrum of severity.
source: Researchers must appreciate that severe malaria is not an objective category but a subjective case definition subset from a spectrum of severity.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: Restricting analyses to specific patient subgroups, especially in the analysis of large pooled datasets, can have a considerable impact on the final result.
source: Moreover, restricting analyses to specific patient subgroups, especially in the analysis of large pooled datasets, can have a considerable impact on the final result (Gelman and Loken, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: It would be very helpful if investigators could publish reproducible code alongside their analyses.
source: With increased emphasis on providing open access data so that analyses can be evaluated and best use made of clinical research it would be very helpful if investigators could publish reproducible code alongside their analyses.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research practices.

claim: Future genetic epidemiological studies could benefit from use of causal diagrams.
source: Future genetic epidemiological studies could benefit from use of causal diagrams and would be more readily evaluable by provision of accompanying code.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research practices.

claim: Future genetic epidemiological studies would be more readily evaluable by provision of accompanying code.
source: Future genetic epidemiological studies could benefit from use of causal diagrams and would be more readily evaluable by provision of accompanying code.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research practices.

claim: The odds ratios for G6PDd in cases versus controls in males were 0.81 (95% CI: 0.68–0.96) for CM and 1.49 (95% CI: 1.24–1.79) for SMA in Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al. (2014).
source: The odds ratios for G6PDd in cases versus controls are given in Table 3 of Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al. (2014) (page 1201). The results, restricted to males, are 0.81 (95% CI: 0.68–0.96) for CM and 1.49 (95% CI: 1.24–1.79) for SMA.
evidence: This cites specific data from Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al. (2014).

claim: A total of 6283 cases had cerebral malaria or severe malarial anaemia in the Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al. (2014) study, broken down as 3345 had cerebral malaria only; 2196 had severe malarial anaemia only; 742 had both cerebral malaria and severe malarial anaemia.
source: A total of 6283 cases had cerebral malaria or severe malarial anaemia, broken down as 3345 had cerebral malaria only; 2196 had severe malarial anaemia only; 742 had both cerebral malaria and severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This cites specific data from Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al. (2014).

claim: The odds ratios for G6PDd in cases versus controls in males were 0.82 (95% CI: 0.69–0.98) for CM and 1.48 (95% CI: 1.22–1.8) for SMA in Clarke et al. (2017).
source: The odds ratios for G6PDd in cases versus controls are given in Table 3 of Clarke et al. (2017) (page 6). In this publication, the results, restricted to males, are 0.82 (95% CI: 0.69–0.98) for CM and 1.48 (95% CI: 1.22–1.8) for SMA (their Table 3).
evidence: This cites specific data from Clarke et al. (2017).

claim: Clarke et al. (2017) included a total of 6284 patients with cerebral malaria or severe malarial anaemia, broken down as: 3359 individuals had cerebral malaria only; 2184 had severe malarial anaemia only; 741 had both cerebral malaria and severe malarial anaemia.
source: They included a total of 6284 patients with cerebral malaria or severe malarial anaemia, broken down as: 3359 individuals had cerebral malaria only; 2184 had severe malarial anaemia only; 741 had both cerebral malaria and severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This cites specific data from Clarke et al. (2017).

claim: The marginal probability of CM can be estimated as 0.34, independent of G6PD status.
source: From the data in Clarke et al. (2017) and Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al. (2014), we can estimate the marginal probability of CM as 0.34, independent of G6PD status (assumption 2).
evidence: This is a parameter estimated from the prior studies for use in the simulation.

claim: The marginal probability of SMA can be estimated as 0.24.
source: We can also estimate the marginal probability of SMA as 0.24.
evidence: This is a parameter estimated from the prior studies for use in the simulation.

claim: The probability of G6PDd in males was 0.15.
source: The probability of G6PDd in males was 0.15.
evidence: This is a parameter estimated from the prior studies for use in the simulation.

claim: G6PD deficiency is the exposure of interest and cerebral malaria (CM) is the outcome of interest in the causal diagram.
source: G6PD deficiency is the exposure of interest (green) and cerebral malaria (CM) is the outcome of interest (red).
evidence: This describes the causal diagram in Figure 1.

claim: By defining the CM cases as those who had coma but no severe anaemia, collider bias operates on the effect of G6PDd on CM.
source: By defining the CM cases as those who had coma but no severe anaemia, collider bias operates on the effect of G6PDd on CM.
evidence: This is the caption of Figure 1 explaining the collider bias mechanism.
